talks.title: How Contexts Fail (and How to Fix Them)
talks.description:
How Contexts Fail (and How to Fix Them) - Drew Breunig, cmpnd.ai

Million-token context windows promised to make agent-building easy: connect every tool, dump in every document, and let the model sort it out. In practice, the opposite happens. As an agent's context grows, performance degrades in surprising ways. And the failures get worse precisely in the situations agents live in: multi-step tool calls, accumulated history, and information pulled from sources that don't agree with each other.

This talk breaks down the ways long contexts fail using concrete, measured example.

Then we get practical, walking through tactics for fixing your context or preventing failures in the first place, with real results behind each. 

Context is not free. Every token influences the response, for better or worse, and the job of the agent builder is deciding what earns its place.

We'll close with where this is all heading, why the most robust answer to context rot isn't hand-tuning prompts but treating context as something you assemble and compile programmatically, and what that looks like in practice.
talks.whyWatch: Recognize when long context distracts or misleads an agent, then decide what to retrieve, compact, or leave out of the next step.

talks.title: Making Swarm Work: Coordination Primitives for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
talks.description:
Making Swarm Work: Coordination Primitives for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems - Jodee Varney, Cisco

Swarm architectures matter when coordination itself is the hard problem. Central orchestration works well for decomposable tasks with clear authority, but it breaks down in open-ended coordination: multi-party negotiation, conflicting objectives, partial knowledge, dynamic membership, and cases where no single agent has enough context or authority to direct the work.

This session explores what it takes to support peer-to-peer coordination in open source agent systems. Using Mycelium, an open source project we have been working on, we will demo coordination primitives such as agent discovery, intent alignment, constraint negotiation, and shared state across a collectively evolving task.

This session will show where current collaboration features in OpenClaw-style agent systems fall short when agents need to coordinate as peers rather than simply exchange delegated tasks.

Attendees will come away with a clearer understanding of the coordination problems that arise in peer collaboration, practical approaches to address them, use cases where swarm is the right fit, and the infrastructure needed to support swarm patterns.
talks.whyWatch: Compare centralized orchestration with a peer swarm for jobs where agents have partial information, competing objectives, or changing membership.

talks.title: Beyond Chat: Lessons Learned Building Intelligent UIs with MCP Apps
talks.description:
Beyond Chat: Lessons Learned Building Intelligent UIs with MCP Apps - Riley Scheid, Reboot (reboot.dev)

With MCP Apps, AI interactions are no longer limited to text. MCP Apps unlock the full power of the web within AI chat, letting us build AI-enriched UIs that persist, react and collaborate in real-time.

Through demos and code deep-dives, I'll showcase foundational patterns we've found effective as MCP Apps gain ubiquity.

Durability: A "social media management platform" that persists across conversations, threads, and even different AI clients—shared memory that allows collaboration between authors.

Async background tasks: Kick off a long-running process, monitor progress live, and get a completion notification in chat while other work continues. Works even on clients without async MCP support.

Realtime sync: watch the async stream back how done it is as it works to completion.

You'll leave with patterns you can apply to your own MCP Apps today.
talks.whyWatch: Design an interactive MCP App that shares live state while accounting for differences between hosts.

talks.title: Your AI Agent Installed Malware Because a SKILL.md Told It To
talks.description:
Your AI Agent Installed Malware Because a SKILL.md Told It To - Liran Tal, Snyk

That SKILL.md file you just installed to supercharge your AI coding agent? It might be exfiltrating your AWS credentials right now. Yikes. Just like with early npm, attackers are abusing various Agent Skill ecosystems to launch malware campaigns. So now AI builders rush to add Skills which inherit the agent's full execution environment, yet ToxicSkills research found 37% of nearly 4000 skills malware and other security weaknesses, and even one "security scanner" skill that was itself malware, ha! The next AI security frontier is hijacking the agent's own reasoning to suppress safety warnings. Here’s your chance to see in action how coding agents crumble under a malicious skill.

In this session you'll watch live hacking of a malicious skill and how it fools a coding agent for rogue actions, a prompt injection leaks your secrets over email, and a leaky skill passes credit card numbers straight through the LLM context. Then I’ll show you how to detect these malware and dangerous skill.md files and catch what every regex-based scanner misses. You'll leave with a concrete threat model for Agent Skills supply chains.
talks.whyWatch: Treat agent skills as software dependencies and review their trust and permissions before giving them access to a developer environment.

talks.title: Self-Hosting Agents: What Changes When Models Become Infrastructure
talks.description:
Self-Hosting Agents: What Changes When Models Become Infrastructure - Miriah Peterson, SchoolAI

Running open models locally changes how engineers think about agent systems. Once models move from hosted APIs into self-managed infrastructure, problems that were previously hidden behind providers become operational realities: latency, orchestration, throughput, observability, GPU memory, tool-call reliability, evaluation variance, and cost control.

This talk shares lessons learned building and operating self-hosted agent systems with llama.cpp, vLLM, quantized models, local coding agents, and production-like homelab infrastructure. Using examples from Pedro CLI, multi-model serving, evaluation workflows, and distributed inference experiments, we will look at what changes when the model is no longer an API call but part of the platform.

Rather than focusing on benchmarks or hype, this session focuses on the operational work required to make open models useful in agent workflows: routing, retries, context management, observability, quantization tradeoffs, and failure recovery.

Attendees will leave with a practical model for deciding when self-hosting makes sense, what infrastructure problems to expect, and how to design open agent systems that are reliable enough to operate.
talks.whyWatch: Work out what your team must operate when it self-hosts an agent model, from GPU memory and inference throughput to reliable tool calls.

talks.title: Post-Training Is Back
talks.description:
Post-Training Is Back - Ariel Shulman, Nvidia

For the last two years the default answer to "my agent gets this wrong" has been a better prompt, a bigger model or an LLM judge in the loop. Fine-tuning felt like something only labs did. We think that's changing, and the reason is ground truth.

Here is how in under $500 using a single 8xH100 Node and open weights model *REDACTED* running LoRA-SFT we were able to run at 30x less the cost of using a frontier model with similar results.
talks.whyWatch: Decide when training on reliable task examples can improve an enterprise data agent more economically than repeatedly using a larger model.

talks.title: The Agent Has Left the Chat
talks.description:
**Harald Kirschner from Microsoft explains why an AI agent's work gets trapped in the chat window where it started, and how the open Agent Host Protocol (AHP) lets one running session be watched, reviewed, and steered from a laptop, a remote dev box, or a phone. If you have ever waited on an agent that needed your approval while you were away from your computer, this talk shows the fix.**

Topics covered:
- Why sessions get stuck: agents now run for hours, edit files, run terminals, and ask for approval, but each session lives inside one app.
- Standards that worked before: how the Language Server Protocol (LSP) let every editor reuse the same language tooling, and why agents need the same pattern.
- Skills, AGENTS.md, and MCP: shared standards for agent know-how, repository instructions, and tool connections.
- A host that owns the session: a dedicated agent host keeps the live session running, even when the laptop lid closes.
- Multi-client demo: start a plan in VS Code, continue it in the Agents window, and open the same session in a browser on a phone.
- Snapshots and replay: a client that joins gets the full conversation and workspace state, and a reconnecting client replays what it missed.
- Sub-agents and automations: background sub-agents appear as separate chats, and automations can run on the host with no client connected.
- AHP compared with ACP and A2A: many clients to one host (AHP), one agent inside one editor (ACP), and agents handing work to other agents (A2A).
- Beyond the editor: an inbox, a board, and a game-style interface built on the same session state.

This talk is for developers building agent clients, tools, and interfaces, and for anyone who wants agent work to follow them across a laptop, a remote machine, and a phone.

Links and resources:

talks.title: Agent Governance Lives in the OS
talks.description:
Agent Governance Lives in the OS - Alexander Sklar & Roberth Karman, Microsoft

Governance is what we want from agent systems: to know, and prove, what an agent did, what it was allowed to do, and what it could not. Most of the conversation about how to get there happens at the wrong layer: protocol design, permission prompts, system prompts. Those help. They are not enforcement.

What actually decides whether an agent reads your SSH keys is the OS. So, if governance is the goal, OS-level security is the mechanism, not a parallel track or a downstream concern, but the foundation.

This talk takes that seriously. We built Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) because agents needed it: an open-source cross-plat policy runtime that decides, per tool invocation, what files, network, and processes are in scope. It composes with what each OS provides (bubblewrap, seatbelt, AppContainer) rather than replacing them, and lets one policy say something coherent across all three. We will cover where the thesis holds up, where platform primitives do not compose cleanly, and what is not yet solved by any of this, including the agent loop itself.

Production agent systems require this layer. The session is an invitation to shape what it should look like, together.
talks.whyWatch: Understand which controls belong at the operating-system boundary so an agent’s file and process permissions can be enforced and audited.

talks.title: The Agentic Orchestration Stack: Durability, Guardrails, and Attestation
talks.description:
The Agentic Orchestration Stack: Durability, Guardrails, and Attestation - Yaron Schneider, Diagrid

AI agents introduce a fundamentally different orchestration problem. Unlike traditional workflows, agents make decisions at runtime, interact with humans and external systems, and often execute over hours, days, or weeks. Durable execution is a necessary foundation - but durability alone is not enough.

As agents become responsible for increasingly important tasks, organizations need the ability to prove what happened, verify who or what performed an action, enforce policies and guardrails, and establish trust in execution outcomes. This requires a new set of capabilities that go beyond workflow orchestration, including identity-aware execution, cryptographic attestation, execution provenance, and verifiable audit trails.

In this talk, we'll explore the shift from workflow orchestration to agentic orchestration and the architectural patterns emerging to support it. Attendees will learn how durable execution, guardrails, and cryptographically verifiable execution histories work together to make autonomous systems reliable, governable, and trustworthy in production.
talks.whyWatch: Design long-running agent workflows that can recover after interruption, enforce guardrails, and retain verifiable records of what happened.

talks.title: Open Source Software Factories: Building an Operating System for Our Agents
talks.description:
Open Source Software Factories: Building an Operating System for Our Agents - Chris Sells, Gas City, Inc.

An operating system has a few core pieces: a process table, working memory, a file system, and a scheduler, all providing services to apps. An agentic OS needs the same services: work to do (the process table), context (working memory), agentic memory (the file system), and workflows (the scheduler). At Gas City, Inc., we've built an open source agentic OS: Beads tracks the work and memories, and Gas City assembles the context and orchestrates the workflows. In this session, we'll walk through the part that surprised us: a software factory is just one kind of app to run on this agentic OS. We keep building others, including the infrastructure on which we run our whole company.
talks.whyWatch: See how Gas City organizes coding agents around shared work queues, persistent context, and deterministic workflows.

talks.title: Interoperable Agent Discovery: AI Catalog, ARD, and the AGNTCY Directory
talks.description:
Interoperable Agent Discovery: AI Catalog, ARD, and the AGNTCY Directory  - Luca Muscariello, Cisco & Junjie Bu, Google

Multi-agent systems today compose across MCP servers, A2A agents, and agent skills — artifacts that live in separate registries with incompatible metadata formats. AI Catalog addresses this at the standard level: a typed JSON format that gives each artifact type a common envelope for identity, capability, and provenance, without replacing the formats each community has standardized.

What makes the standard operational is federation. AI Catalog's well-known discovery mechanism lets clients traverse distributed registries without a central index. ARD complements it with a user-facing API — enabling any code assistant (Claude, Copilot, Gemini) to discover AgentSkills, MCP servers, and A2A cards across federated catalogs, verify them cryptographically, and resolve them to a live endpoint without knowing the source registry.

The AGNTCY directory implements content management, multi-registry discovery, and federation end to end. We demo the full flow: publishing an AgentSkill, an MCP server, and an A2A card under the AI Catalog standard, federating them through ARD, and discovering them securely from a code assistant at runtime.
talks.whyWatch: Compare how AI Catalog and the AGNTCY Directory describe and discover agents, skills, and servers while retaining provenance for verification.

talks.title: When Agents Spawn Agents: Securing Recursive Delegation in Multi-Agent Systems
talks.description:
When Agents Spawn Agents: Securing Recursive Delegation in Multi-Agent Systems - Anishma Mavuram, EmpowerID

Enterprise agentic systems are moving from single assistants to agent chains: Agent A spawns B, B delegates to C, and C invokes an MCP tool that writes to a system of record. The unit of risk is no longer just the tool call — it is the delegation edge. The key question: is each descendant operating within a valid, revocable, least-privilege authority chain tracing back to a consenting human or root principal?

Without that zero-trust chain, teams face confused-deputy attacks, delegation laundering, privilege creep, forged lineage, and audit trails that cannot prove who authorized what.

This session presents RDCP — the Recursive Delegation Capability Profile — a standards-first pattern for securing recursive delegation. RDCP composes identity, authorization, policy, revocation, and evidence standards into a practical control-plane architecture.

We will show cryptographic identity, signed spawn intent, grant-before-token issuance, OAuth Token Exchange/RAR, DPoP or mTLS child tokens, monotonic least-privilege attenuation, AuthZEN PDP decisions, MCP Gateway enforcement, subtree revocation, and tamper-evident receipts linking spawn → delegation → token issuance → tool call → outcome.
talks.whyWatch: Design delegated permissions so an agent that spawns another agent can pass on narrowly scoped, revocable access with an auditable chain.

talks.title: Decentralized Discovery: MCP, Skills, and Beyond with AI Catalog
talks.description:
Decentralized Discovery: MCP, Skills, and Beyond with AI Catalog - Tadas Antanavicius, Warp.dev

Agents, when equipped with the right Skills and MCP servers, can accomplish nearly any task a human can do with a computer. Today, that typically involves one notable pre-requisite: human-initiated pre-installation of those Skills and MCP servers.

The new AI Catalog standard developed in collaboration between individuals from Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Cisco, and others paves a path to eliminating that pre-requisite. By rallying around a standardized .well-known/ai-catalog.json URI, agents like Claude.ai, Claude Code, Goose, and others can accomplish mid-session discovery of artifacts like Skills and MCP servers. For example, if you didn't know a GitHub MCP server existed (or how to connect to it) when you asked your coding agent to perform a PR review, your coding agent can now automatically discover that MCP server and offer to install and connect to it before it even starts the review.

This dynamic unlocks a new service discovery economy embedded into agentic workflow UX we're already using. Instead of requiring users to have advance knowledge of what MCP servers they might want their coding agent to have access to, now their agents can recommend highly relevant services with a one-click installation experience.

Attend this session to learn the specifics of how this mechanism works, its limitations, and what's next.
talks.whyWatch: See how an agent could discover MCP servers and skills through structured publisher catalogs without relying on one centralized registry.

talks.title: 1,149 Hackers Tried to Break Our AI Agent Guardrails. 0 Succeeded. Here's Why.
talks.description:
1,149 Hackers Tried to Break Our AI Agent Guardrails. 0 Succeeded. Here's Why. - Uchi Uchibeke, APort

Every agent framework gives your AI tools. None of them ask: "should this agent be allowed to use this tool right now?"
We built an open-source pre-action authorization layer that intercepts tool calls before execution - not in the prompt, but in the framework hook. Then we let 1,149 people try to break it in a public CTF. Attack success rate dropped from 74.6% to 0%.

Outline:
1) The architectural gap: Why post-hoc guardrails (NeMo, Guardrails AI) can't prevent actions they only detect - and why pre-action authorization is a different layer entirely

2) The OAP spec: How the Open Agent Passport works - agent identity, capability-scoped policies, and Ed25519-signed decisions at ~65ms p50

3) Live CTF data: What 1,149 attackers actually tried, which attack patterns worked against unprotected agents, and why deterministic policy enforcement stopped all of them

4)The convergence: Why three independent groups (APort, Microsoft AGT, Airia) shipped the same architectural pattern within weeks of each other - and what that means for the stack

5)Live demo: I'll configure a passport, attach it to Claude Code, and show an allow and a deny in real-time with the audit trail
talks.whyWatch: Learn where to place deterministic authorization checks so sensitive tool calls are reviewed before the agent executes them.

talks.title: Breaking the Agentic Loop - Multi-Turn Exploits Against Tool-Using AI Agents
talks.description:
Breaking the Agentic Loop - Multi-Turn Exploits Against Tool-Using AI Agents - Bar Kaduri, Capsule Security

Single prompts are yesterday's problem. Real agents live inside an agentic loop: plan → act → observe → update state → repeat. That loop is exactly where attacks hide, spread across turns, disguised as "reasonable" steps, and amplified by tools, skills, and memory.

Most current red teaming approaches ignore this structure. They treat agents like chatbots and probe them with individual prompts. In practice, the most damaging failures rarely appear in a single step. They emerge gradually as the attacker steers the loop across several turns.

In this talk we red team agents white box. Instead of blindly probing prompts, we model the internal structure of the agent and generate adversarial interaction trees that manipulate it across multiple turns.

The resulting exploits do not rely on a single malicious instruction. Individually reasonable actions accumulate into a compromise as the attacker bends the planning process, poisons memory, manipulates tool outputs, and chains safe operations into unsafe outcomes.

We'll demo several multi-turn exploit patterns, including memory poisoning, tool and skill output injection, planner steering & privilege escalation through chained tool calls.
talks.whyWatch: Assess whether your agent’s defenses hold across a sequence of tool calls, where individually acceptable actions can combine into an unsafe outcome.

talks.title: The Model Proposes, the Server Decides: Shipping a Payment MCP Server to Hosts You Don’t Control
talks.description:
The Model Proposes, the Server Decides: Shipping a Payment MCP Server to Hosts You Don’t Control - Antoni Kozelski, Vstorm & Bartosz Gonczarek, VStorm

We built a production-grade MCP server that lets an AI assistant configure, quote, and order printed products and send a payment link. Connected to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and Codex, it behaved four different ways: some hosts cut or ignored our instructions, some could not show the payment button, and one sometimes used its own tools instead of ours. This talk explores those differences, why rules for irreversible steps now live in the server rather than the model, and how the server handles a large product catalog without exposing it to the client. It also covers how these lessons led us to contribute to open-source frameworks and projects.
talks.whyWatch: Decide which ordering and payment checks an MCP server must enforce itself when different hosts interpret its tool responses differently.

talks.title: Your Agent Sandbox Is Built Backwards
talks.description:
Your Agent Sandbox Is Built Backwards - Dan Fernandez, Edera & Ariadne Conill, Edera, Inc.

Most agent security starts with broad authority and chips away at it: pre-approved command lists, destructive-action warnings, trust tiers wrapping a shell. Claude Code is the most sophisticated public version of this subtractive model, and it is excellent engineering. The trouble is the model. You have to anticipate every dangerous thing an agent might do, and agents decide what they do at runtime.

An older idea from operating-systems security inverts it. Start the agent with zero authority and inject scoped capability objects. There is no policy to bypass, because authority that was never minted cannot be invoked. An agent cannot hallucinate past a capability it was never given.

We will trace what the additive model takes in practice: capabilities minted narrow, narrowed further when delegated, and gone after a single use. The lifecycle that grants authority is also the audit trail, which beats reconstructing which policy was active when something went wrong. You will leave able to tell whether your own agent starts from everything or from nothing.
talks.whyWatch: Compare starting an agent sandbox with zero permissions against starting with broad access and trying to block dangerous actions afterward.

talks.title: Mapping Industry Representation and Gaps in Agentic AI Standards
talks.description:
Mapping Industry Representation and Gaps in Agentic AI Standards - Jake Pineda, The Linux Foundation

In under a year, the Agentic AI Foundation reached 300 members. We will categorize contributors, maintainers, and funders by industry. We will highlight strong industry representation and identify gaps that need closing. Those who shape standards like MCP, AGENTS.md, AgentGateway, Agent Router A2A and goose define whose needs are met. If key industries teams stay absent, they risk inheriting mismatched specifications and costly workarounds. Attendees will learn which sectors lack a voice and how your organization can get involved.
talks.whyWatch: Identify which sectors are missing from agent standards working groups and how that affects the use cases those standards support.

talks.title: ID-JAG: Solving OAuth Sprawl for Enterprise AI Agents
talks.description:
ID-JAG: Solving OAuth Sprawl for Enterprise AI Agents - Aaron Parecki, Okta & Den Delimarsky, Anthropic

Enterprise AI agents are moving from demos into production, and auth is becoming a blocker. Demo agents can connect to tools with OAuth, but real enterprise agents may need SaaS services for thousands of employees. Per-user, per-service consent does not scale.

This session explains ID-JAG, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant pattern behind MCP's Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension. ID-JAG turns an existing SSO login into centrally governed, auditable access to approved MCP servers, without repeated OAuth prompts.

We'll cover the production problem, protocol flow, and lessons from implementing ID-JAG support in Archestra, one of the first MCP clients to support it. We'll also discuss what identity provider support enables.

Attendees will leave with a model for production agent auth: one SSO login, centralized policy, scoped MCP-native access tokens, fewer consent screens, and a cleaner security review story.

We'll close with the missing piece: SaaS provider adoption. To unlock enterprise deployments, authorization servers need to support this flow so agents can access approved business systems without key-sharing, manual credentials, or one-off integrations.
talks.whyWatch: Understand how ID-JAG can reuse enterprise identity-provider trust for MCP authorization instead of prompting every user for consent to every service.

talks.title: From AI Assistants to Trusted SDLC Agents: FINRA’s Agentic Engineering Journey
talks.description:
From AI Assistants to Trusted SDLC Agents: FINRA’s Agentic Engineering Journey - Geetha Ramachandran, FINRA

At FINRA, the move from AI assistants to agentic engineering required more than better prompts. It required custom agents with bounded responsibilities, MCP-based integration into enterprise SDLC tooling, and design patterns that keep humans in control while agents reduce repetitive engineering work.

This session shares how FINRA is building practical agentic workflows: guarded tool access, explicit context, observability, reusable skills, and MCP integration across repositories, CI/CD, and workflow systems. It will also discuss how an Agent Skills campaign, skills catalog, and enablement model helped turn experimentation into shared capability rather than one-off solutions.

Using SDLC use cases such as technology upgrades as examples, this talk will show what it takes to move from IDE-centric assistance to trusted, context-aware agents that are composable, observable, reusable, and fit for enterprise software delivery.
talks.whyWatch: See how FINRA integrates bounded agents for test generation and dependency upgrades while keeping humans in control of code changes.

talks.title: x401: HTTP Proof Requirement Protocol
talks.description:
x401: HTTP Proof Requirement Protocol - Ian Macallister, Proof

Ian Macallister is EVP of Strategy and Business Development at Proof, the company behind x401, the open HTTP protocol that lets any website ask an AI agent to prove who it’s acting for before it acts. x401 shipped to production this month with contributors from OpenAI, Visa, Okta, Circle, Lightspark, and MATTR. Proof, the company that creates legal identities to secure high assurance transactions on the internet, recently launched the ability to enable x401 natively through Cloudflare and their partnership with Circle. He’s here to show you how the handshake works and how to put it in front of your own endpoints.
talks.whyWatch: Understand how an HTTP identity challenge can ask an agent for verifiable evidence of who it represents before accepting a transaction.

talks.title: Is Your Agent Any Good? Lessons From a Wide and a Deep Deployment
talks.description:
Is Your Agent Any Good? Lessons From a Wide and a Deep Deployment - Ethan Lo & Jason Jiang, Adaptive Security

One of our agents knows its false positive rate to the decimal. For the other few hundred, 🤷‍♂️

That's the gap between two teams at Adaptive Security, an AI cybersecurity startup. AI Enablement (Ethan) rolled out agents to 200+ people in every department. One of the most popular was built by our head of CS over a weekend, and it ran on a Mac mini until it kept falling over. Email Security (Jason) built a detection pipeline that answers one question: is this email malicious?

Both teams ended up doing the same four things: find the judge (the person who can tell a good answer from a bad one), build the agent, design the eval loop, and improve iteratively. We just did them in a different order. Jason built the evaluation tooling before anything shipped. Ethan shipped first and figured out the eval loop later (it ended up being Slack emoji reactions).

We'll cover what each order got us, how we decide when a change is safe to make, and what broke when nobody was looking.
talks.whyWatch: Compare how to evaluate a broad internal agent rollout and a narrowly scoped email classifier with measurable false positives.

talks.title: Beyond Scraping: Building Agent-Ready Documentation Layers for MCP and AI Agents
talks.description:
Beyond Scraping: Building Agent-Ready Documentation Layers for MCP and AI Agents - Ayodeji Ogundare, Adyen

Most developer documentation portals are still built for humans first. That worked when developers read the docs directly. It creates friction when they use AI agents and code assistants to solve implementation problems while coding.

Server log analysis of over 10 million requests on docs.adyen.com showed that 11.6% of traffic came from AI bots. 78% of generative AI traffic came from user-directed assistants pulling context for active coding tasks.

Developers are no longer only reading documentation. They are asking AI tools to interpret it, reason over it, and turn it into working code.
The problem is that standard web documentation isn't designed for this workflow. HTML pages and site hierarchies waste model context as bots crawl, guess, and reconstruct structure.
We addressed this by turning static docs into agent-ready markdown infrastructure.

We added /llms.txt for structured LLM discovery, exposed raw content through .md URLs, and packaged a full documentation mirror as a ZIP file.

This session shares how to move from human-centric HTML to machine-consumable markdown, reducing traversal overhead, avoiding unnecessary rate limits, and improving AI-generated integration code.
talks.whyWatch: Make developer docs easier for coding agents to discover and read while keeping the underlying examples accurate.

talks.title: Stop Writing Agents, Declare Them: Declarative Agent Architecture in Production
talks.description:
Stop Writing Agents, Declare Them: Declarative Agent Architecture in Production - Chris Knuteson, A Place For Mom

Most teams build an AI agent the way they'd regret building a service: one prompt doing seven jobs. Every requirement is another paragraph, every change risks regressing the rest, and the only unit of isolation is the whole agent. You can't prompt your way out of that shape.

The alternative, which we run in production for Grace, a senior-living advisor: stop writing agents - declare them. An AgentSpec is a small, versioned contract - one spec, one agent, one job. What it leaves out is the point. Provider, model, budget, and killswitch live on a per-agent gateway key, not in the spec; prompts live in a registry; tools are refs. That narrow waist buys three things by construction: governance (authority declared, enforced, and audited per agent), resilience (kill one key and exactly one agent stops; safety stays synchronous), and future-proofing (swap model or runtime with zero spec change). One spec is served over web, agent-to-agent, and as an MCP server - the platform itself becomes a tool any MCP client can call.

You'll leave with the contract, the gateway-as-policy-plane pattern, and an honest account of what's shipped versus still ahead.
talks.whyWatch: See how a versioned AgentSpec defines one agent’s job while a separate gateway key controls its model, budget, and permissions.

talks.title: Open Source Has Been Here Before: Sustainability Lessons for Agentic AI
talks.description:
Open Source Has Been Here Before: Sustainability Lessons for Agentic AI - Katherine Druckman, JetBrains

MCP crossed 110 million SDK downloads a month, with well over ten thousand servers. The agentic ecosystem is scaling faster than almost anything open source has seen, and a surprising amount of what agents depend on in production runs on single maintainers and on reference servers that shipped as demos and quietly became infrastructure.

Open source has lived versions of this before: a single maintainer carrying a package with hundreds of thousands of weekly downloads, the cURL project pulling its bug bounty under a flood of AI-generated reports that overwhelmed a small volunteer team. Every dependency an agent relies on becomes a responsibility, and someone is carrying that load.

Agentic AI concentrates the social contract open source has always run on, because these dependencies now sit underneath software that acts on its own, calling tools and moving data. What used to be a hidden flaw is now one an agent will act on, at machine speed. We'll talk about supporting maintainers, making contribution the default, narrowing the gap between who consumes and who gives back, and staying responsible humans while the standards are still being shaped.
talks.whyWatch: Check who maintains the open-source tools your agents rely on and whether those projects can sustain production use.

talks.title: Context Is the Substrate: Production Patterns for Knowledge-Graph-Backed Agents
talks.description:
Context Is the Substrate: Production Patterns for Knowledge-Graph-Backed Agents - Cassie Shum, Praxa, Inc

Coding agents can open a pull request in minutes. Whether that change is correct, traceable, and worth keeping is a different problem, and it is the one that decides whether an agent fleet is an asset or a liability in production.

This talk shares patterns from running a knowledge-graph-backed agent fleet in production, where humans and agents work on the same codebase, on the same timeline, against the same audit log. 
Here are some examples of those patterns:

-Context as a bundle: assemble everything a task needs up front, instead of letting the agent retrieve chunk by chunk at query time.
-Provenance as working memory: an audit trail the agent reads to know what it did to understand why a decision was made.
-Code as truth: reconcile intent and reality
- Visibility as a query: treat throughput, context size, cost, and audit completeness.

A recurring theme: agents are a fast, honest mirror of your engineering culture. The same fleet, pointed at a healthy codebase and a brittle one, produces very different outcomes at identical speed. We close on where this connects to MCP, AGENTS.md, and the broader push toward structured, interoperable context.
talks.whyWatch: See how shared context graphs and audit trails can help coding agents preserve task intent across a fleet working on the same codebase.

talks.title: Your Agents Need a Router: One Integration for Every Model and Tool
talks.description:
Your Agents Need a Router: One Integration for Every Model and Tool - Varun Talwar, Tetrate

Every agent starts simple: one model, one SDK, a demo that works. Then comes the second provider, the MCP tools, the fallback logic, the rate-limit backoff — and suddenly half your codebase is integration glue that has nothing to do with what your agent actually does.

Agent Router — newly donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, with a 1.0 GA release and production deployments at scale — collapses all of it into a single integration: every model, every tool, one declarative API.

We'll walk through a live agent workload end-to-end: routing across model providers with automatic failover; understanding exactly what each agent and team spends — and capping it before it surprises you; and choosing which MCP tools each agent can see and call. All declared in one place, none of it in your application code. You'll leave knowing exactly where a router fits in your agent stack, what it takes to run one in production, and how to get involved in the Agent Router project.
talks.whyWatch: Move provider routing, fallbacks, and tool access into one gateway so individual agents carry less integration code.

talks.title: Building an Agentic Eval Pipeline: Battle-Tested Lessons with EvalBench
talks.description:
Agents look impressive in a demo, then quietly get worse after a small change to a prompt, tool, or skill. In this talk, Kurtis Van Gent and Haoyu Wang of Google Cloud Databases explain how to test an AI agent on real user journeys so you catch breaks before your users do. They share lessons from building EvalBench, an open-source evaluation framework that grew from NL2SQL testing into complex agent workflows.

Kurtis is an MCP core maintainer and leads the transport working group. Kurtis and Haoyu both work on Google Cloud Databases.

Topics covered:
- Why unit tests fall short: They confirm that code runs, but not whether an agent uses the tool correctly, in the right order, with the right result.
- Critical user journeys (CUJs): Tasks written the way a user would ask for them, such as "Show me my top customers," not as instructions to call a specific tool. The same evals run against Claude Code, Codex, and other agents.
- Multi-turn journeys: A simulated user answers follow-up questions, such as which region matters, so the agent is tested across the whole conversation.
- Grading the path and the outcome: Check which tools were called, in what order, whether extra calls were made, and whether the cloud resources ended up in the expected state.
- Explainable LLM judges: Use deterministic checks first, such as running a golden query and comparing the data. Use structured scorecards for the rest, and calibrate them against human raters.
- Reliable eval infrastructure: Each run starts from a known state, gets scored, and resets its resources so one run cannot leak into the next.
- Token cost of tools and skills: Large tool schemas and dozens of skills cost tokens before the agent does any work. Evals show whether tool search or truncated skill descriptions hurt goal completion.
- Ablation tests: Run the same journeys with and without a skill to see whether it improves completion, saves tokens, or only adds cost.
- Long-running operations: While an agent polls for a database to finish creating, every check costs tokens. MCP tasks let the harness wait and get notified when the work is done.

If you build MCP tools, agent skills, or AI agents, this talk shows how to measure whether each change makes your agent better or worse. Try EvalBench on your own tools and skills, and star the project on GitHub if it helps.

talks.title: Stop Agents From Leaking Your Secrets - AI Hooks To The Rescue
talks.description:
Stop Agents From Leaking Your Secrets - AI Hooks To The Rescue - Dwayne McDaniel, GitGuardian

Git gives us a way to automate just about anything. With Git hooks and off-the-shelf security tools, developers have been able to weave all sorts of checks into their Git rituals, 'shifting left' in order to eliminate security rework later. But Git was made for humans, and only the commit was meant to be shared. 

Today, coding assistants like Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot can read files, propose changes, run commands, and interact with project context, often across a messy workspace. In an agentic workflow, secrets leak through context, output, and history.
Fortunately, these tools have started supporting AI hooks, which allow you to move your testing closer to when the code and development artifacts are produced. 

Come to this session if you want to learn: 

 - How hooks provide a practical pattern for catching mistakes before they leave a developer’s machine.
 - Why AI coding tools like Cursor, Claude, and Copilot need guardrails beyond prompts and trust.
 - How to use AI hooks, rules, and automated checks before agents edit files, run commands, or touch sensitive systems.
 - How teams can reduce risk, improve consistency, and make safer contribution paths the default.
talks.whyWatch: Use deterministic pre-tool checks and secret scanning to reduce the chance that a coding assistant reads or shares credentials.

talks.title: Beyond LLMs in a Loop: Building Trusted Agents in Regulated Industries
talks.description:
Beyond LLMs in a Loop: Building Trusted Agents in Regulated Industries - Lucas Beeler, Aerospike

Most agentic systems in regulated industries face the same challenge: compliance, legal, and audit teams often reject deployment once they understand how LLMs make decisions. The popular “LLM calls tools in a loop” architecture is poorly suited for HIPAA, SOX, PCI-DSS, and similar requirements. Guardrails can reduce known risks, but they cannot guarantee compliance, safe behavior, or auditable outcomes.

This session presents an alternative architecture for trusted agents. Rather than placing the LLM at the center of decision-making, the model is limited to tasks such as translating human intent into specifications. Core reasoning is performed by deterministic systems using classical AI techniques, including knowledge representation, formal verification, and constraint-satisfaction solvers.

Using a production HIPAA-compliant healthcare staffing agent as a case study, the talk shows how natural-language requests become verified specifications, how staffing plans are generated, and how audit-ready evidence is maintained. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for building compliant, trustworthy agents in regulated environments.
talks.whyWatch: Separate LLM planning from policy validation so regulated workflows can verify constraints and retain evidence before acting.

talks.title: Architecting Agentic Commerce: The Universal Commerce Protocol and Agent Payments Protocol
talks.description:
Architecting Agentic Commerce: The Universal Commerce Protocol and Agent Payments Protocol - Amit Handa & Shonan Shah, Google

Discover how Google is leveraging the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to build the future of AI-driven shopping. This session explores how UCP powers features beyond Checkout like Universal Cart to operate smoothly across surfaces such as Search, Gemini, YouTube, and Gmail. We will go deeper into how UCP's discovery and pluggable capabilities-based architecture enables frictionless shopping experiences and reduces custom integrations.

Additionally, we will dive into UCP's expansion as a transactional backbone and detail how AP2 secures "Human Not Present" agentic payments through cryptographic proof of user intent. Attendees will leave with actionable takeaways, including the latest technical specifications, an understanding of the security models for agentic flows, and a clear road map for adopting the open protocols that will power the next generation of retail.
talks.whyWatch: Follow an agent purchase through capability discovery, checkout, and authorized payment to see which responsibilities UCP and AP2 handle.

talks.title: The Agentic Web for Industry Verticals
talks.description:
The Agentic Web for Industry Verticals - Andrew Nolan, Microsoft

Tools for agents are important, but how will industries with unique scenarios, risks, and obligations serve their customers at scale?

Drawing on his work as co-creator of WebMCP and chair of the Agentic AI Foundation's Applied Industries Committee, Andrew Nolan explores the challenges industries face in adopting the agentic web and how innovators and leaders are working to address them.

Attendees will leave with a clearer picture of where the agentic web has unique needs, what slows adoption at industry scale, and how to bring their own use cases into the conversation.
talks.whyWatch: Identify what industry teams need beyond WebMCP before they can expose customer workflows with appropriate data permissions and trust controls.

talks.title: Agentic State Machines: Turning an Agent Loop into an Experimentation Platform
talks.description:
Agentic State Machines: Turning an Agent Loop into an Experimentation Platform - Douwe Osinga, Block

Agent loops started simple: ask a model what to do, run a tool and return the result. As agents gained approvals, context management, hooks, skills, retries and steering, that loop became a tangle of concerns influencing one another.

This talk explains how goose replaced its central loop with a re-entrant state machine. The conversation is the state, and independent but cooperative Operations inspect that state and return effects. We will look at what this changes for cancellation, persistence and testing, then follow a real experiment: using a decision model to select reasoning effort for each user turn. The experiment remains one removable Operation; inference and tool execution never need to know it exists.

The result is not only cleaner architecture. It turns goose into a platform where new agent behaviors can be tested without first redesigning the entire agent.
talks.whyWatch: Turn a sprawling agent loop into a resumable state machine so approvals, tool calls, and retries can be tested independently.

talks.title: Shipping Agent Skills Safely: CI/CD, Evals, and Guardrails
talks.description:
Shipping Agent Skills Safely: CI/CD, Evals, and Guardrails - Michael Larson, Christensen Solutions

Agent skills, prompts, workflow instructions, and attached assets are quickly becoming things teams share, reuse, and depend on. But in many organizations, these are still copied around like helpful notes instead of treated like software that can break, drift, or create risk.

This session looks at what it means to build CI/CD for agent skills before rolling them out across an organization. We will cover practical ways to test whether a skill still works, run regression evals, check common failure modes, review tool permissions, test for prompt injection in skill files and assets, and safely roll out changes.

The goal is to move beyond “this prompt seemed to work for me” toward a disciplined engineering workflow for agent skills. Attendees will leave with a practical model for versioning, testing, validating, shipping, and improving agent skills so teams can adopt agentic workflows without creating compounding reliability or security problems.
talks.whyWatch: Test and version shared agent skills like software so teams can catch regressions before releasing changes to prompts or instructions.

talks.title: The Agentic SDLC: How We Shipped AI-Native Software at a Legacy Company
talks.description:
The Agentic SDLC: How We Shipped AI-Native Software at a Legacy Company - Austin Brown, A Place for Mom

A Place for Mom has served senior care families for 20 years. In 2025 we built a B2C home care platform — AI-native from the first commit. Not "we added Copilot." Every layer runs with agentic tooling: planning, coding, review, deployment, observability. In production since November 2025.

July 2025 through May 2026: 3,478 PRs across four repos, 2,822 merged, 81% merge rate.

We built a five-layer stack. CLAUDE.md files give agents persistent context so they aren't starting fresh each session. Structured planning prevents the 200-lines-down-the-wrong-path failure mode. Git worktrees let parallel sessions run in isolation. A 10-stage multi-agent review pipeline with confidence scoring vets every PR. And platform-mcp — a Go service connecting Claude to New Relic, PagerDuty, Jira, GitHub, AWS, and Databricks through one endpoint — replaced six integrations.

The harder question is what that pace does to comprehension. Velocity is measurable. Understanding is not. When an engineer ships in two hours what took two days, do they understand it well enough to debug it at 2am? 

We call this comprehension debt — and the guardrails built for code quality are the best defense.
talks.whyWatch: See how a legacy company used agent tooling across planning, review, deployment, and operations while building a new consumer product.

talks.title: MCP Apps + WebMCP - The Next Era of Interface
talks.description:
MCP Apps + WebMCP - The Next Era of Interface - Liad Yosef, MCP Apps, Dominic Farolino, Google, Sarah Drasner, Google & Olivier Chafik, Anthropic

WebMCP is a way for an agent to interact with your website / UI.

MCP Apps are a way for a server to return UI to be displayed in the agent - for visualization, branding and the “last mile of interaction”.
These two technologies sit on both sides of the agentic-UI spectrum, and combining them completes the full cycle of human-agentic interactions.

By combining WebMCP with MCP Apps, you can expose your capabilities directly to an agent that rides alongside the user. This also allows the agent to use WebMCP to control an MCP Apps UI.

Walk away from this session with the ability to use WebMCP to let an agent drive your existing website, learn how to expose specific site functions (like "Compare Pricing") that the agent can render as an interactive, on-the-fly widget inside a chat sidecar with MCP Apps and build flows where the user handles the visual interaction, and the agent handles the heavy lifting. Understand the use cases and best practices for WebMCP and MCP Apps, and see how combining them usher in the new era of interfaces.
talks.whyWatch: Decide when a website should expose tools through WebMCP and when an agent host should display an interactive interface through MCP Apps.

talks.title: Superpowering ChatGPT with mcp Extensions
talks.description:
Superpowering ChatGPT with mcp Extensions - Victor Lin, OpenAI

In this talk, we’ll explore how OpenAI is enabling developer plugins that feel like first-class features of ChatGPT through plugin extensions, announced at DevDay. We’ll trace the journey from introducing the Apps SDK and helping shape MCP Apps last year to launching plugin extensions this year. We’ll showcase key use cases, discuss where these extensions could fit into the MCP and MCP Apps standards, and share what we’ve learned from iterating on the spec with internal teams and external developers.
talks.whyWatch: See what ChatGPT plugin extensions add to MCP Apps and which use cases benefit from an interface integrated into the host.

talks.title: Workshop: Keep Infrastructure Out of Your AI Agents and MCP Servers
talks.description:
Workshop: Keep Infrastructure Out of Your AI Agents and MCP Servers - Lin Sun & Christian Posta, Solo.io

As AI agents move to production, engineering teams face a growing set of challenges. How do you secure and govern MCP servers without modifying them? Route and fail over across multiple LLM providers? Enforce rate limits, access controls, and governance policies? Observe agent traffic, manage context growth, and scale operations across environments?

Rather than embedding these capabilities into every agent, MCP server, and application, organizations can adopt a single architectural pattern: the agent gateway.
An agent gateway acts as a unified control plane for AI systems. It can function as an MCP gateway, LLM gateway, inference gateway, and traditional API gateway, centralizing security, observability, routing, resilience, and policy enforcement across agents, tools, models, and services.

In this hands-on workshop, you'll learn how to secure and federate MCP servers without code changes, route and fail over LLM traffic across providers, enforce authentication and usage policies, and gain end-to-end visibility into agent interactions. Through live demos, you'll see how a single gateway layer simplifies operations while enabling secure, scalable, and governable AI systems.

talks.title: Workshop: The Buzz-Word Is Collaboration 🐝
talks.description:
Workshop: The Buzz-Word Is Collaboration - Morgan Martin, Wes Billman, Bradley  Axen, Tyler Longwell & Lucas Isaza, Block

Most teams made a person the API between their agents and everyone else: copy the output into chat, paste the reply back into the harness. This hands-on workshop shows the alternative: put the agents where the work is. We use Buzz, Block's open source, channel-driven workspace where people and AI agents share conversations, repositories, and reviews.

We begin in the middle of a live project, with four people and a swarm of agents working across shared channels and code. Then we rewind and bring the room in. Attendees will join a shared Buzz community, work with an agent, form channels with other participants, and practice delegating, steering, reviewing, and coordinating work as it happens. Along the way, we examine how Buzz approaches portable identity, scoped capabilities, signed work, and collaboration across different agent runtimes and models.

By the end, the room itself becomes part of the workflow: everyone contributes code, assets, and reviews to one shared project in a Buzz-hosted Git repository. Bring a laptop. Leave with practical experience running many agents in one shared workspace, where the whole team can see, steer, and use them.

**Space Limited - First Come, First Served.  Please bring a fully charged laptop to the workshop**
talks.whyWatch: See how an open-source shared workspace can keep human and agent collaboration in the same channels and threads.

talks.title: Workshop: Hands-on A2A: Service Discovery and Multi-Agent Delegation
talks.description:
Workshop: Hands-on A2A: Service Discovery and Multi-Agent Delegation - Pedro Melendez, Sergio Villani & Sirisha Karra, Google

This 75-minute interactive workshop provides a hands-on environment for engineers to explore agent-to-agent (A2A) protocols through practical execution rather than product pitches. Key takeaways and exercises include:

  - Building & Publishing Agent Cards: Attendees configure and publish agent cards to expose capabilities securely.
  - Dynamic Discovery & Delegation: Participants discover peer agents via card metadata and delegate complex tasks in real time without upfront schema agreements.
  - Handling Real-World Objections: The lab directly addresses common protocol objections through immersive scenarios.

*Infrastructure & Approach:*

  - Environment: We will use GCP as our standard infrastructure for workshops, leveraging pre-deployed agents on Cloud Run within isolated attendee projects to minimize custom setup.
  - Protocol Focus: Emphasizes generic, open-source (OSS) solutions and vendor-neutral, protocol-level mechanics rather than specific product surfaces.

*Space Limited - First Come, First Served. Please bring a fully charged laptop to the workshop*
talks.whyWatch: Practice publishing an A2A Agent Card and delegating a task to another agent through a shared protocol.

talks.title: How AT&T Is Building an Agentic Front Door for Enterprise HR
talks.description:
How AT&T Is Building an Agentic Front Door for Enterprise HR - Natalie Gilbert, AT&T, Sherman Bell, AT&T, Emily Williams, AT&T, Hector Tejada, AT&T Services, Inc. & Prateek Baranwal, AT&T

AT&T, an enterprise with 130,000 employees, has a sprawling HR ecosystem that spans many environments, policies, teams and business processes. As a result, even basic HR tasks can be difficult to navigate efficiently. So, AT&T is building an agentic front door for HR, Ask AT&T for HR, to map employee needs to practical process workflows. Unlike many AI solutions, this is not a Q&A chatbot that simply redirects users to other systems. It's a complex, multi-agent system with secure, live integrations into backend HR systems. The platform uses an orchestrator to coordinate 100+ agents, each mapped to a distinct business process. The architecture combines publicly available and bespoke MCPs to connect agents to various enterprise systems, allowing agents to perform HR-related tasks within a single user interface.

This session will focus on the cutting-edge architecture behind Ask AT&T for HR, which relies on reusable workflow patterns, MCP tools that connect to backend systems, deep agents that communicate via an orchestrator, and a SOX-compliant task engine that sends tasks to designated employees while allowing paused workflows to resume where they left off once the task is complete.
talks.whyWatch: See how AT&T routes HR requests to specialized agents while a separate task engine handles human approvals and audit records.

talks.title: Cut The Noise: Building a Code Reviewer You Can Trust
talks.description:
Engineering teams now have agents writing code faster than people can review it. When an AI reviewer posts too many wrong findings, people stop reading what it says. In this talk, Joah Gerstenberg of Block, Inc. explains how Block rebuilt its AI code reviewer to favor precision, so the comments that reach developers are ones worth acting on.

Topics covered:
- Verification as the bottleneck: once models could write trustworthy code, checking that code became the hard part.
- Code review as a ritual of trust: reviewers at Block now handle about three times as many lines of code as they did a year ago.
- Measuring against human reviews: a test corpus of expert reviews sets the bar, but human comments are not what the model should copy.
- The worst comment: an April bug exposed the reviewer's learned behavior, and Block shut the reviewer down for a week to rebuild it.
- Precision before recall: fewer, correct findings earn trust, and the address rate rose as precision improved.
- Specialist reviewers and a judge: several reviewers inspect a change, a coordinator tries to disprove their findings, and a judge reviews what was dropped.
- Risk-based routing: low-risk changes get a cheaper review and high-risk changes get a deeper one, based on privacy, security, money movement, and SOX compliance.
- Open source: block/review follows this architecture with six review agents.
- Alignment and containment: agents need the wider business context, and the talk also covers Buzz, Block's open source platform for teams and agents.

This talk is for engineers who review AI-written code, teams building AI code reviewers, and leaders deciding how much to trust agents in production.

talks.title: Multi-Agent SRE: What Happens When Your Agents Want Opposite Things
talks.description:
Multi-Agent SRE: What Happens When Your Agents Want Opposite Things - Aditi Mewada, Apple

As SRE teams adopt multi-agent systems, a new class of problem emerges: agents with conflicting objectives operating on the same infrastructure at the same time. Your remediation agent wants to spin up three new nodes to absorb a traffic spike. Your cost-optimization agent wants to terminate underutilized instances to hit budget targets. Both are correct. Both are about to make things worse.

This talk explores the real-world failure modes of multi-agent SRE systems - what happens when agents act on stale state, override each other's changes, or reach a deadlock - and how to design your way out of it. We'll cover conflict detection, priority hierarchies, shared state management, and when to hand control back to a human.
You'll leave with practical patterns for building multi-agent systems that disagree productively, rather than destructively.
talks.whyWatch: Design a deterministic referee for cases where cost and reliability agents try to change the same production resources at once.

talks.title: Are We Ready? Security in a Headless World
talks.description:
Are We Ready? Security in a Headless World - Dexter Horthy, HumanLayer, Ian Livingstone, Keycard, Allie Howe, Keycard, Andrew Becherer, Socket & Scott Johnston, Fly.io

As software becomes something agents call directly through APIs, MCP endpoints, and tools, the human-facing UI may become optional. But the UI did more for security than we gave it credit for: it constrained actions, showed humans what they were authorizing, and added friction before mistakes compounded.

This panel debates whether a headless future is inevitable, whether it makes software more or less secure, and what replaces the security functions the UI once provided. If agents become the new interface, identity, authorization, and audit trails may have to take its place.
talks.whyWatch: Identify which consent and authorization controls need replacing when an agent calls a service directly and skips the human-facing UI.

talks.title: Why Domain-specific Agents Are the Future
talks.description:
Justin Schroeder of Standard Agents argues that AI work should be split into small, domain-specific agents, each built for one business process, instead of one giant model handed every task. He explains why integration, trust, and efficacy push businesses this way, and what has to exist before it works at scale.

Topics covered:
- Why one giant model with skills and MCP looks like an old factory
- Domain-specific agents: tiny agents built around one or two small tasks
- What an agent is, in plain terms
- Why businesses build agents anyway: integration, trust, and efficacy
- Why a Gmail agent is more dependable than a Gmail skill
- Efficacy: scoping an agent to one business process makes it easier to evaluate
- Token spend, and cheaper models that handle narrow tasks well
